name: Outdoor and hot workplaces
intro: People who cannot stop working when it is hot: builders, vendors, riders, farm, factory and sanitation workers.

problems.q: Safe drinking water costs too much
Home stays hot after the shift
Warnings don’t reach us in a useful way
No one local to install or fix it

problemsSource.label: People’s Courage International: Hot Cities Make Hard Work Harder, a study with workers in Delhi, Kathmandu, Dhaka, Jakarta and Quezon City

cards.title: Worker cooling stations
cards.what: Rest points where workers already are, with shade or cooling, seating, drinking water, rehydration salts, a first-aid kit and a way to reach a clinic.
cards.protects: Construction workers, vendors, drivers, porters and loaders between jobs or on breaks.
cards.suits: Construction sites, markets, bus and taxi stands, labour chowks and community spaces with heavy foot traffic.
cards.running: Water, ice and salts every day; cleaning; power for fans; someone on site; repairs before each season.
delivery: On the routes workers really use, not where land happens to be free
Matched to working hours, including early mornings and evenings
Shade or cooling, safe water, seating, first aid, referral to a clinic
A named person who checks, cleans, refills and repairs it
Lost wages, permission to leave work, disability access, who feels welcome
Visits, days open, user views, and health or income outcomes measured properly

evidence.text: The Migrants Resilience Collaborative reported that more than 27,000 workers used its cooling stations in India, Nepal and Bangladesh in one summer. These are the programme’s own figures; health and income effects have not been independently measured.

source.label: People’s Courage International, 2025: emergency response to the heatwave crisis in South and Southeast Asia

examples.text: At a Bengaluru construction site, a station cooled with water-soaked khus panels drew about 100–120 workers a day in April, falling to 70–80 after the monsoon began.

source.label: The Migration Story

examples.text: In 2026, People’s Courage International ran 20 cooling centres in big cities, placed near construction sites, road junctions and the labour nakas where day-wage workers look for jobs, with water, rehydration salts and phone charging. It reported more than 88,000 visits, and up to 1,841 in a day at one centre. These are the programme’s own figures.

source.label: World Economic Forum and BCG, Workforce Heat Resilience: An Actionable Framework to Close the Execution Gap, 2026

cards.stops: A station nobody can leave work to use, or one that closes when the day is hottest.
worksIf: Employers let workers use it without losing pay
It is open when people work
Someone refills and repairs it every day

cards.title: Warnings that reach workers
cards.what: Route official alerts through trusted worker messengers, voice notes and picture boards at stalls and labour chowks, with one clear action in each message and a way to report back.
cards.protects: Vendors, labourers and anyone without a smartphone, signal or the time to read.
cards.suits: Markets, labour chowks and worker unions or associations with leaders people trust.
cards.running: A messenger’s time every alert day, printed boards, and someone who answers when workers report a problem.

evidence.text: In Delhi in 2025, the India Meteorological Department, worker organisations and Greenpeace India set up colour-coded heat boards at vending carts and sent bilingual audio and text alerts on WhatsApp to more than 20 worker leaders, who passed them on.

source.label: Greenpeace India: inside India’s first community-led early warning system for informal workers

examples.text: Vendors call themselves ‘climate messengers’; workers who cannot read ask them what the board means.

source.label: Mongabay India, July 2025

cards.stops: Alerts that tell people to stay indoors when they cannot, and no one listening when they report back.
worksIf: Each message comes with an action people can take
A named messenger passes it on
Workers can report missing water, shade or help, and someone responds

cards.title: Safe water people do not have to buy
cards.what: Free or cheap drinking water close to where people live and work: piped connections, community water points or refill stations.
cards.protects: Workers and families who now buy water and drink less than they need when it costs too much.
cards.suits: Informal settlements and work areas where water has to be bought.
cards.running: Upkeep of pipes and points, water quality testing, and a fair way to bill or share costs.

evidence.text: In Dhaka, the city water utility worked with local NGOs to bring 3,000 water connections into informal settlements through mini-networks joined to the city system.

source.label: Agence Française de Développement: improving access to drinking water in Dhaka’s informal settlements

cards.stops: Rules that tie a connection to land title, so people in informal settlements cannot get one.
worksIf: Connections do not require land title
Water is tested and safe
Someone local can fix a broken point fast

cards.title: Local jobs to install and keep it working
cards.what: Train and pay local people to install, run and repair cool roofs, water points, shade and green spaces.
cards.protects: Everyone who depends on the equipment working, and the workers who gain a skill and income.
cards.suits: Any programme that builds things that need upkeep.
cards.running: Wages and training, built into the running budget from the start.

evidence.text: Community-run drinking water plants in Delhi’s low-income settlements created local jobs in running the plants and distributing water.

source.label: Kumar, 2024: water security through the Tata Power DDL RO water plants

cards.stops: Projects that train people once and then stop paying them.
worksIf: Upkeep jobs are paid for every year
Training leads to real work

cards.title: Portable shade where there is no wall or tree
cards.what: A light shelter with a bench and shade that can be moved between work sites or fixed to a wall.
cards.protects: Outdoor workers at sites with no shade at all.
cards.suits: Short-term sites, roadsides and markets.
cards.running: Moving and fixing it, and repairs; someone needs to own it.

evidence.text: Bengaluru’s Neralu shelter won a 2024 design contest: about 15 kg, seats four, costs about US$175, and can be carried on an auto-rickshaw. It had not yet been tried by workers when it was shown in May 2025.

source.label: AP News, June 2025, via KSAT

examples.text: In Rewa, Madhya Pradesh, a ₹5,000 grant from the All India Disaster Mitigation Institute let a fruit and vegetable seller buy a large umbrella covering him and his produce, and a way to keep drinking water on his cart, so he no longer had to leave to find water. In Kolkata, a movable plastic sheet gave shade to a utensil seller with no fixed pitch.

source.label: AIDMI, southasiadisasters.net Issue 228: Small Heat Resilience Measures, Big Impact in Small Towns and on Small Businesses in India, 2026

cards.stops: Nobody owning it once the pilot ends.
worksIf: Workers test the design first
Someone owns, moves and repairs it

cards.title: Paid rest breaks that switch on with the alert
cards.what: Agree rest, shade and water breaks that start automatically at each alert level, with earlier or split shifts on the hottest days.
cards.protects: Construction, farm, delivery, sanitation and street workers.
cards.suits: Any worksite where an employer, contractor or city department sets the hours.
cards.running: Little equipment; the cost is paid time. Someone has to check the rule is kept.

evidence.text: In Singapore, monitors at 24 workplaces found workers could face more heat stress than nearby weather stations reported, so set breaks by heat measured on site.

source.label: NUS Project HeatSafe, 2024

examples.text: Outside Asia, at a sugar producer in Nicaragua, a rest, shade and water programme with La Isla Network raised cane-cutters’ productivity by 19% over five harvests despite shorter days, and cut hospital-treated acute kidney injury by 94%. Pay was changed so workers did not lose money by resting.

source.label: Hansson et al., Annals of Work Exposures and Health, 2024

examples.text: The same programme was estimated to return about $1.60 for every $1 invested by its third year.

source.label: World Economic Forum and BCG, Workforce Heat Resilience: An Actionable Framework to Close the Execution Gap, 2026

examples.text: In October 2026, the Philippines’ Department of Labor and Employment said it was preparing heat safety measures for delivery riders with platform operators, using heat-index levels to guide breaks and when work stops. Its 2023 labour advisory already asks employers for adjusted rest breaks, free drinking water and ventilation.

source.label: Philippine Daily Inquirer, October 2026

examples.text: Among 287 sugarcane cutters in Nakhon Sawan, Thailand, each 1 °C rise in heat stress (WBGT, measured in the fields over a whole shift) cut output by about 9 stalks an hour, from an average of 387.

source.label: Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health, 2026

cards.stops: Piece-rate pay and fixed deadlines that make stopping cost money, and no inspection.
worksIf: Breaks are paid, or paired with income protection
Heat is measured where people work
Shade and water are a few minutes away
Inspectors or unions can check

cards.title: Shade and water on work routes
cards.what: Rest shelters with seating, drinking water and rehydration salts along the streets and yards where people work.
cards.protects: Street vendors, delivery riders, traffic police, sanitation and construction workers.
cards.suits: Busy junctions, markets and work yards. Misting only in dry, breezy spots.
cards.running: A daily refill and cleaning roster, often ₹500–2,000 a day per water point, and repairs before each season.

evidence.text: Nagpur put shade nets over 10–12 busy junctions in May 2026; several tore or collapsed in strong winds, and residents pointed out the heat had begun at the end of March.

source.label: The Hitavada, 11 May 2026

cards.stops: Nobody named to refill and repair it, or it goes up after the heat has started.
worksIf: It is in place before the hot season
A named team refills and repairs it
Workers are allowed to stop and use it
Frames are fixed firmly for storms

cards.title: Income protection when it is too hot to work
cards.what: Cash that pays out automatically when heat crosses a set threshold, so workers can afford to stop.
cards.protects: Informal and daily-wage workers, especially women.
cards.suits: Where workers belong to an association, cooperative or scheme that can enrol them and pay by phone.
cards.running: Premiums or a public subsidy every season, plus enrolment and payment systems.

evidence.text: In a survey of informal workers in Bangkok, nearly 80% had cut their hours because of heat.

source.label: WIEGO and HomeNet Thailand, 2025

examples.text: In 2026, about 17,000 informal workers in South Asia were covered by parametric heat insurance arranged through People’s Courage International and a local partner, most with premiums paid by companies. Each payout was set at about ₹1,000–3,000, enough for 5–6 days of basic needs, with up to ₹9,000 over a year. These are the programme’s own figures.

source.label: World Economic Forum and BCG, Workforce Heat Resilience: An Actionable Framework to Close the Execution Gap, 2026

cards.stops: A trigger that misses the heat people feel, so they are harmed without a payout, and slow payments.
worksIf: The trigger counts humidity, not only temperature
Money arrives within days
Workers know they are covered

cards.title: Heat-illness first aid on every shift
cards.what: Train supervisors and co-workers to spot heat illness, cool a person fast and get help, with water, shade and ice at hand.
cards.protects: Everyone on the site, especially new and older workers.
cards.suits: Construction sites, factories, brick kilns and farms with a supervisor.
cards.running: A refresher before each season, and a steady supply of water and ice.

evidence.text: Doctors at two Indian hospitals with heatstroke units said more than 90% of the patients they treated for heat illness in 2024 were outdoor workers.

source.label: Context (Thomson Reuters Foundation), 2024

examples.text: Most worker heat illness strikes early: about 80% happens in the first four days on the job. Guidance is to build up new and returning workers’ hours in the heat over 7–14 days, with stricter limits during heatwaves.

source.label: World Economic Forum and BCG, Workforce Heat Resilience: An Actionable Framework to Close the Execution Gap, 2026

cards.stops: Training given once and forgotten, and no transport to a clinic.
worksIf: Someone trained is on every shift
Everyone knows the emergency number
Treatment is free at the clinic

cards.title: Measure and cool hot sheds and factories
cards.what: Measure heat at the workstations, then cool the roof and walls, add air flow, water and breaks.
cards.protects: Garment, factory, kiln and warehouse workers, many of them women.
cards.suits: Indoor workplaces under metal roofs or beside furnaces.
cards.running: A heat meter and someone to read it daily; upkeep of roofs and fans; power for ventilation.

evidence.text: At three garment factories in Phnom Penh, workers reporting heat symptoms rose from 68% in the cooler months to 88% in the hot months, by their own reports.

source.label: Chea et al., BMC Public Health, 2025

examples.text: Studies summarised for apparel buyers find output falls about 2.6% for each degree of heat stress above 24 °C WBGT. Where toilets are unsafe or missing, women workers often drink less water and suffer worse heat illness, so toilets belong in the plan.

source.label: FSG, Managing Heat: From Worker Welfare to Business Resilience, 2026

cards.stops: Nobody measuring heat indoors, and factory owners who rent the building.
worksIf: Heat is measured where people stand
Workers can report symptoms without risk
Fans have power when it is hottest

name: Homes
intro: Where people sleep, cook and care for others, often under thin roofs that stay hot after dark.

cards.title: Cool roofs
cards.what: A white, solar-reflective coating on tin, asbestos or concrete roofs, so less heat reaches the room below.
cards.protects: Families in informal and low-income homes, older people, young children and the sick.
cards.suits: Sound roofs in hot, sunny places, where residents can stay long enough to benefit.
cards.running: Recoating every few years, and a thermometer to check it works.

evidence.text: In a two-year trial in Burkina Faso, cool roofs lowered indoor temperatures by 1.2–1.7 °C and residents’ heart rates fell; a trial in about 400 Ahmedabad homes began in 2025.

source.label: Reuters, via South China Morning Post, 2025

examples.text: In Dhaka’s Kerail settlement, reflective paint went on 105 buildings, including a day care centre, a school and two garment factories. Indoor air at peak heat fell by 7.72 °C in one building and by 3.5 °C on average; one roof’s surface fell by 12.3 °C. Thin corrugated roofs made it hard to apply, and some local paints were not reflective enough.

source.label: Sustainable Energy for All and the Kigali Cooling Efficiency Program, via PreventionWeb, 2021

examples.text: In an industrial building in Indonesia, a 5,200 m² cool roof brought indoor air at noon down from 40.8 °C to 30.4 °C for about 500 shift workers. These are indoor air readings; roof-surface drops are always larger.

source.label: Sustainable Energy for All and the Kigali Cooling Efficiency Program, via PreventionWeb, 2021

cards.stops: Promising degrees nobody measured, renters who cannot change the roof, and no money to recoat.
worksIf: Rooms are measured before and after
Tenants are protected from rent rises
Someone pays to recoat

cards.title: Shade the walls and let the air through
cards.what: Bamboo blinds, jute screens or awnings on the sunny side, and higher vents that let hot air out at night.
cards.protects: Everyone indoors, especially at night.
cards.suits: Most homes; screens are cheap and households can fit them.
cards.running: Fixing and replacing screens each season; vents need rain and mosquito screens.

evidence.text: In low-income homes measured in Dhaka, Delhi, Faisalabad and rural Maharashtra, tin-roofed houses stayed warmer indoors than outside because they cooled so slowly at night.

source.label: Tasgaonkar et al., Scientific Data, 2022

cards.stops: Openings that let in dust, rain or intruders, and screens that block all air.
worksIf: Air can still move
Vents are secure
Someone replaces worn screens

cards.title: Fans and power people can afford
cards.what: Efficient fans, lifeline electricity tariffs and reliable supply in the hottest weeks.
cards.protects: Low-income households without any way to cool down.
cards.suits: Homes with a grid connection; solar where the grid is weak.
cards.running: Monthly power bills, and a grid that holds in a heatwave.

evidence.text: 1.12 billion of the rural and urban poor are at high risk because they lack access to cooling.

source.label: Sustainable Energy for All, 2023

cards.stops: Power cuts at the hottest hours, and bills people cannot pay.
worksIf: Power is reliable when it is hottest
Tariffs protect the poorest
Fans are efficient

cards.title: Cooler, cleaner kitchens
cards.what: Let heat and smoke out of the kitchen, move cooking to cooler hours, and make cleaner fuel affordable through the season.
cards.protects: Women and girls who cook, and children near the stove.
cards.suits: Homes cooking indoors on wood, dung, kerosene or gas.
cards.running: Fuel costs every month, and upkeep of vents and chimneys.

evidence.text: In Nepal’s Madhesh Province, women cooking in hot, smoky kitchens carry a daily ‘thermal labour’ that falls hardest on women in the poorest single-room homes with little access to clean energy or credit.

source.label: Ghimire and others, Frontiers in Public Health, 2025

cards.stops: Clean fuel bought once but not refilled, and kitchens with no way for air to escape.
worksIf: Refills stay affordable all season
There is an opening for heat and smoke
Women decide how it is designed

cards.title: Check on people alone through hot nights
cards.what: Neighbours, health workers or volunteers call or visit older, ill and disabled people who live alone, day and night, during alerts.
cards.protects: Older people, people with disabilities or long-term illness, people living alone.
cards.suits: Any neighbourhood with a list of who lives alone.
cards.running: A list kept up to date, and volunteers’ or health workers’ time during alerts.

evidence.text: Data from 47,628 people in 68 countries shows hot nights shorten sleep, with bigger losses for older people and in lower-income countries.

source.label: Minor et al., One Earth, 2022

cards.stops: No list of who lives alone, and calls that stop at sunset.
worksIf: Someone keeps the list
Calls continue after dark
Callers know when to send help

name: Schools and childcare
intro: Children in hot classrooms learn less and fall ill more easily. Most fixes are small and seasonal.

cards.title: Cool the hottest classrooms first
cards.what: A reflective coating or a ventilated second roof over the classrooms that get hottest.
cards.protects: Pupils and teachers.
cards.suits: Single-storey schools with metal or concrete roofs.
cards.running: A line in the school maintenance budget for recoating; anchors checked before the monsoon.

evidence.text: In the United States, each 1 °F hotter school year without air conditioning cut that year’s learning by about 1%, with the largest losses for disadvantaged students. Effects in Asian classrooms are not yet measured.

source.label: Park, Goodman, Hurwitz and Smith, American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2020

cards.stops: Canopies not anchored for monsoon winds, and no budget to recoat.
worksIf: Classroom heat is logged before and after
There is money to maintain it

cards.title: Water, and time to drink it
cards.what: Enough safe, cool drinking water for every child, with breaks in the timetable to use it.
cards.protects: Every pupil, especially the youngest.
cards.suits: Every school.
cards.running: Filter changes, cleaning and a supply that lasts the hottest weeks.

evidence.text: Heatwaves disrupted schooling for an estimated 171 million students in 2024, and South Asia was the most affected region.

source.label: UNICEF, 2025

cards.stops: One tap for hundreds of children, or filters nobody changes.
worksIf: Enough taps for the number of children
Teachers build drinking into the day

cards.title: Heat-ready timetables
cards.what: Start earlier, shorten the hottest afternoons, move exams and sports, and keep learning going if schools have to close.
cards.protects: Pupils, teachers and parents who travel in the heat.
cards.suits: Education departments and school boards, set before the season.
cards.running: Little money; it needs agreed triggers and a plan for remote or make-up learning.

evidence.text: Bangladesh closed schools for about 33 million children in its April 2024 heatwave, and Cambodia cut the school day by two hours.

source.label: NBC News, 2024

cards.stops: Closing schools with no plan for learning, and decisions made on the day.
worksIf: Triggers are agreed before the season
There is a plan to make up lost learning

cards.title: Shaded play space
cards.what: Trees, shade structures and less hard paving where children play and queue.
cards.protects: Children at break times and assembly.
cards.suits: Schools with open yards and a water source.
cards.running: Watering through the holidays, when nobody is at school.

evidence.text: Researchers studying how age groups use green spaces found children wanted trees for shade and places to play: ask them before you design.

source.label: Frantzeskaki et al., chapter 11 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023

cards.stops: Planting that dies in the first summer break.
worksIf: Someone waters through the holidays
Children help choose where shade goes

name: Health facilities
intro: Clinics and hospitals fill up in a heatwave just as power, water and staff come under strain.

cards.title: Ready to cool heatstroke patients fast
cards.what: Rapid assessment and active cooling of suspected heatstroke, with ice packs, IV fluids, rehydration salts and trained staff.
cards.protects: Anyone with heat illness, above all outdoor workers and older people.
cards.suits: Every hospital and health centre in heat-prone districts.
cards.running: Stocks of ice, fluids and medicines through the season, and training every year.

evidence.text: In June 2024 India’s health ministry asked central government hospitals to set up special heatwave units, and advised rapid assessment and active cooling of suspected heatstroke, with stocks of rehydration salts, IV fluids and ice packs.

source.label: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India, press release, 19 June 2024

cards.stops: Supplies that run out at the peak, and staff who have never practised the protocol.
worksIf: Staff train before the season
Ice and fluids are stocked early
Care for heat illness is free

cards.title: Keep the power on and the building cool
cards.what: Backup or solar power, cooling in waiting and treatment areas, and cool roofs, shading and rainwater harvesting.
cards.protects: Patients, staff, and medicines and vaccines that spoil in heat.
cards.suits: Facilities on weak grids or under hot roofs, especially in rural areas.
cards.running: Fuel or battery upkeep, servicing of cooling, and a power company that prioritises the facility.

evidence.text: About 12% of health facilities in low- and lower-middle-income countries in South Asia have no electricity at all, and rural facilities are worse served than urban ones.

source.label: WHO fact sheet: electricity in health-care facilities, 2023

cards.stops: Backup generators with no fuel budget, and cooling nobody services.
worksIf: The power company knows the facility comes first
Someone services the backup
There is a running budget

cards.title: Protect the staff
cards.what: Cool rest rooms, drinking water, and shorter rotations for staff in full protective gear.
cards.protects: Nurses, doctors, community health workers and cleaners.
cards.suits: Wards, emergency rooms and outreach teams in hot weather.
cards.running: Staff time for rotations, and a cooled rest space.

evidence.text: Across 3,082 health workers in India, Indonesia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam, poor practices with protective equipment were linked to heat-related symptoms.

source.label: Yang et al., BMC Nursing, 2024

cards.stops: Too few staff to rotate during a surge.
worksIf: Rotas plan for the surge
Staff can report symptoms early

cards.title: A surge plan linked to the warning
cards.what: Extra beds, staff and supplies that switch on with each alert level, agreed with the weather service and the city.
cards.protects: Everyone who falls ill in a heatwave.
cards.suits: District and city health systems with a heat warning.
cards.running: Planning time before the season, and overtime or reserve staff during alerts.

evidence.text: After Ahmedabad’s heat action plan prepared hospitals and warned the public, an estimated 1,190 deaths a year were avoided.

source.label: Hess et al., Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2018

cards.stops: Warnings that reach the public but not the hospital.
worksIf: Hospitals receive the alert directly
Each level names what the hospital does

cards.title: Shade and water for people waiting outside
cards.what: Shade, seating and drinking water where patients queue, and appointment slots so fewer wait at midday.
cards.protects: Patients and carers, especially older people, pregnant women and children.
cards.suits: Outpatient departments, health centres and vaccination days.
cards.running: Someone to refill water and keep the space usable.

evidence.text: India’s June 2024 advisory asked facilities in heat-prone areas to provide shade outside, and cooling in waiting areas.

source.label: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India, press release, 19 June 2024

cards.stops: Shade built where the queue isn’t.
worksIf: It is where people actually wait
Someone refills the water

name: Markets and neighbourhoods
intro: The streets, markets, stops and public spaces where people spend the hottest hours.

cards.title: Shade and water in markets, designed with vendors
cards.what: Shade over stalls and aisles, and drinking water points, planned and run with the vendors’ association.
cards.protects: Street vendors and their customers.
cards.suits: Open and street markets.
cards.running: Storm-proof fixing, replacing worn cloth, and a refill and cleaning roster.

evidence.text: Of 721 Delhi street vendors surveyed in April and May 2024, 80% saw fewer customers during heatwaves and 49% lost income.

source.label: Greenpeace India and National Hawkers Federation, 2024

examples.text: Young women vendors in Ahmedabad, who already sell 8 to 12 and 4 to 8 to avoid the midday heat, asked for shared shade sails covering about ten sellers each, and a licensed, fixed place to sell.

source.label: AIDMI, southasiadisasters.net Issue 228: Small Heat Resilience Measures, Big Impact in Small Towns and on Small Businesses in India, 2026

cards.stops: Beautification that pushes informal vendors out, and shade that blocks fire access.
worksIf: Vendors have a say in design and upkeep
Nobody is evicted to make room

cards.title: Cool waiting points
cards.what: Shade, a bench, drinking water and the heat alert on a board, at bus stops, ration shops and other queues.
cards.protects: Commuters, older and disabled people, carers with children.
cards.suits: Busy stops and queues with no shade.
cards.running: Refilling the water, and keeping access clear for wheelchairs.

evidence.text: Measuring how hot people feel on summer days, researchers found shade from buildings cooled most by day, then trees, then light structures such as sails.

source.label: Middel et al., 50 Grades of Shade, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society

cards.stops: Counting shelters built instead of people protected.
worksIf: It is where people actually wait
Older and disabled people can reach it

cards.title: Cooling centres people can actually use
cards.what: Cool public spaces, such as libraries, community halls or places of worship, opened during alerts, with water and somewhere to sit.
cards.protects: People with no cool place at home, and outdoor workers on breaks.
cards.suits: Neighbourhoods with many hot homes and a suitable public building nearby.
cards.running: Staff, power and water for every alert day, and transport for those who cannot walk there.

evidence.text: A review of the evidence and strategies for running cooling centres to prevent heat-related illness.

source.label: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in the GHHIN resource library

cards.stops: A cooled building nobody can reach, open at the wrong hours, or a worker who cannot leave work to use it.
worksIf: People can reach it, including those who can’t walk far
It opens at the right hours, evenings too
Power and water are secure
Someone staffs and funds it
Workers are free to leave work to use it

cards.title: Trees that survive
cards.what: Look after existing trees first; plant heat-hardy species where people walk and wait, with water and three years of care.
cards.protects: Pedestrians, vendors and everyone waiting outside.
cards.suits: Streets and open spaces with root space and a water source.
cards.running: Watering and care for at least three years after planting.

evidence.text: In one Berlin park more than 500 of 870 new trees died within ten years despite watering: count trees that survive, not saplings planted.

source.label: Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023

examples.text: Keep wetlands as well as trees: a model of the 2023 heatwave in Cambodia’s lower Mekong delta found wetlands cooled the air by about 2–3 °C over wet areas and beyond, so draining them adds to heat.

source.label: Frontiers in Climate, 2026 (model study)

cards.stops: No water plan, and counting saplings instead of canopy.
worksIf: Water is secured before planting
Someone is paid to care for them
Greening doesn’t push residents out

name: Before summer: for municipalities
intro: The decisions a city or district makes before the first heatwave decide what happens during it.

cards.title: Name an owner and set aside the money
cards.what: Give heat a named lead office, and ring-fence a heat budget before the season starts.
cards.protects: Everyone the plan covers, by making sure it can be paid for.
cards.suits: Every city, district or state with a heat plan, or about to write one.
cards.running: A budget line each year, and staff time in the lead office.

evidence.text: Of 37 Indian heat action plans reviewed, 11 discussed funding, and 8 of those simply asked departments to find their own money.

source.label: Centre for Policy Research, 2023

cards.stops: A plan with no money and no single owner.
worksIf: The money is set aside before the heat
One office answers for the plan

cards.title: Set local alert levels, and who acts at each
cards.what: Set thresholds from local health records, and agree who decides, who acts, who pays and by when at each level.
cards.protects: Everyone, by turning warnings into action.
cards.suits: Cities and districts with a weather forecast and health data.
cards.running: A yearly review of thresholds and who does what.

evidence.text: Ahmedabad set its alert temperatures from the local link between daily maximum temperature and deaths; in 2023 only about 10 of 37 Indian heat plans appeared to set local thresholds.

source.label: Centre for Policy Research, 2023

cards.stops: A warning with no named person to act on it.
worksIf: Every level has someone named to act
Warnings reach people without phones

cards.title: Map who is most exposed, with them
cards.what: Find the neighbourhoods, workers and households most at risk, by walking the area with residents and their organisations.
cards.protects: The people a plan usually misses.
cards.suits: Every ward or district, before choosing actions.
cards.running: A few weeks of fieldwork, updated every year or two.

evidence.text: Of the 37 Indian heat action plans reviewed, only two included a vulnerability assessment.

source.label: Centre for Policy Research, 2023

examples.text: Mapping matters because heat stress is not rising evenly: in Bangladesh the heat index rose fastest, about 0.67 °C a decade over 1981–2023, in 14 north-western districts of Rajshahi and Rangpur, where humidity rose too.

source.label: Discover Hazards, 2026

cards.stops: Mapping from an office, without the people at risk.
worksIf: Residents and workers take part
The map changes what gets built

cards.title: Get the assets ready before the heat
cards.what: Shade, water points, cooling spaces and roof coatings installed and tested by the end of winter.
cards.protects: Outdoor workers, people in hot homes, people waiting outside.
cards.suits: Any city with a known hot season.
cards.running: Upkeep through the season, with named teams and a budget.

evidence.text: Nagpur’s junction shade nets went up in May 2026, though residents said the heat had begun at the end of March.

source.label: The Hitavada, 11 May 2026

cards.stops: Procurement that starts when the heat does.
worksIf: Contracts are signed in winter
Every asset has someone to keep it working

cards.title: Prepare clinics, and count heat illness
cards.what: Check clinics are ready, and record heat illness and deaths every day of the season so the plan can respond.
cards.protects: Everyone who falls ill, and future plans that need the numbers.
cards.suits: District health offices and hospitals.
cards.running: Daily reporting through the season, and training for doctors who certify deaths.

evidence.text: India’s surveillance logged 48,385 suspected heatstroke cases by 28 July 2024, but only 185 confirmed heatstroke deaths.

source.label: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, reply in India’s Rajya Sabha, 6 August 2024

cards.stops: Deaths recorded as heart failure, so heat stays invisible.
worksIf: Doctors know how to record heat as a cause
Numbers are reviewed during the season

cards.title: Release money on the forecast
cards.what: Agree in advance what money is released, and for what, when the forecast crosses a threshold, before the heat peaks.
cards.protects: People who would otherwise get help only after the damage.
cards.suits: Cities and districts with a reliable forecast and a pre-agreed fund.
cards.running: A fund topped up each year, and rules for releasing it.

evidence.text: US$800 million spent on early warning systems in developing countries could avoid US$3–16 billion in losses every year.

source.label: Global Commission on Adaptation, 2019

examples.text: In Dhaka, the Red Cross and Red Crescent tested heatwave triggers in a 2021 simulation and gave cash grants of BDT 4,500; most recipients spent it on food, and many on medical costs. In April 2024 the Bangladesh Red Crescent activated its heatwave early action protocol for real.

source.label: Anticipation Hub: the story of heatwave anticipatory action in Dhaka

cards.stops: Money that needs a declared disaster before it can move.
worksIf: Release rules are agreed in advance
Money reaches people within days
